why-ladder-safety.title: Why Ladder Safety Matters
why-ladder-safety.content: Ladders are one of the most common tools on construction sites, but they are also one of the most frequently misused. A fall from even a relatively low height can result in broken bones, head injuries, spinal injuries, or death. Ladder hazards are often underestimated because ladders are so familiar. Most ladder incidents are preventable when workers follow safe selection, inspection, setup, and climbing practices. OSHA's construction ladder requirements under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart X are intended to reduce fall hazards and ensure ladders are safe for employee use. Training helps workers understand both how to use ladders correctly and what unsafe conditions look like.

ladder-selection.title: Choosing the Right Ladder
ladder-selection.content: Different ladders are designed for different tasks. Straight ladders and extension ladders are used for access to roofs, landings, and platforms. Stepladders must be fully opened and locked before use. Fixed ladders are permanently attached to a structure. Workers must consider ladder height, reach, surface, angle, and duty rating before selecting a ladder. The total load on a ladder includes the worker's body weight plus all tools, materials, and equipment — not body weight alone. Metal ladders conduct electricity and must not be used near energized wiring or power lines; nonconductive fiberglass ladders are required in those situations. A ladder that is too short should be replaced with the correct ladder rather than improvised.

inspection-setup.title: Inspecting and Setting Up Ladders
inspection-setup.content: Ladders must be inspected before each use for cracked, bent, broken, loose, or missing rungs; split or damaged side rails; missing or worn non-slip safety feet; oil, grease, mud, or other slippery substances; damaged ropes, pulleys, or locks on extension ladders; damaged spreaders or braces on stepladders; and missing or unreadable labels. Defective ladders must be removed from service and tagged. For setup, ladders must be placed on firm, level, dry surfaces with feet positioned firmly. The 4-to-1 ratio positions straight and extension ladders at the correct angle: the base should be approximately 1 foot out from the wall for every 4 feet of working height. Never place a ladder where it can be struck by doors, vehicles, or workers — lock or block doors and use barricades or a spotter in high-traffic areas. The top of the ladder should extend sufficiently above the landing for safe transition.

climbing-techniques.title: Climbing and Working Safely
climbing-techniques.content: Always face the ladder while climbing up or down. Maintain three points of contact at all times — two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand. Climb slowly and deliberately. Keep hands free while climbing by using a tool belt or hoisting materials after reaching the work position. Keep your body centered between the rails and follow the 'belt buckle rule': keep your belt buckle between the ladder side rails at all times. Do not overreach, lean backward, or lean sideways. Do not stand on the top rungs of an extension ladder or the top steps or top cap of a stepladder. Only one person should be on a ladder unless it is specifically designed for two-person use. If you cannot reach the work area without leaning outside the rails, climb down and reposition the ladder.

hazardous-conditions.title: When Not to Climb
hazardous-conditions.content: Certain conditions make ladder use unsafe and require stopping work until conditions are corrected. Do not climb a ladder when: the ladder is damaged or defective; weather such as rain, high wind, ice, or lightning is present; the ladder, shoes, hands, or rungs are wet, oily, muddy, or slippery; a metal ladder is near energized electrical equipment or power lines; the worker is ill, dizzy, fatigued, impaired, or taking medication that causes drowsiness; the ladder cannot be stabilized at the correct angle; or the task requires reaching, force, material handling, or body positioning that cannot be done safely from a ladder. In those cases, use nonconductive ladders, postpone work until weather clears, or substitute a scaffold or aerial lift for the task.

fixed-ladders.title: Fixed Ladders, Moving, and Storage
fixed-ladders.content: Fixed ladders are permanently attached to structures and must be inspected before climbing for corrosion, loose or damaged rungs, and deterioration around connections. OSHA requires fall protection — such as safety cages, ladder safety devices, or self-retracting lifelines — for fixed ladders with climbs equal to or exceeding 24 feet under 29 CFR 1926.1053(a)(19). When carrying ladders, move them horizontally at your side when possible, get help for long or heavy ladders, and watch for overhead power lines, workers, vehicles, equipment, and building materials. Lower a ladder before moving it whenever possible. Store ladders in a dry, protected location where they cannot fall, warp, or create tripping hazards. Never leave ladders raised or unattended after use.

fall-response.title: Fall Response and Reporting
fall-response.content: If a worker falls from a ladder, call for medical assistance immediately. Do not move the injured person unless they are in immediate danger — movement can worsen head, neck, back, or spinal injuries. Monitor breathing and responsiveness. Control serious bleeding if trained to do so. Watch for signs of shock. Secure the area to prevent additional injuries and preserve the scene for investigation. Report the incident according to company procedures. Near misses — incidents that could have caused injury under slightly different circumstances — must also be reported. A sliding ladder base, a nearly dropped tool, or a slipping foot are all near misses requiring corrective action before someone is hurt. Reporting near misses allows supervisors to fix problems before an injury occurs.

1.questionText: Before stepping onto a ladder, what should a worker do first?

options.text: Place the ladder and begin climbing slowly to check stability
Verify a coworker is available to hold the base
Choose an appropriate ladder and inspect it for defects
Check the weather forecast before making any other decisions

2.questionText: When assessing ladder load capacity, only the worker's body weight needs to be considered.

options.text: True
False

3.questionText: Using the 4-to-1 ladder ratio, if a ladder's working height is 16 feet, how far should the base be from the wall?

options.text: 1 foot
2 feet
4 feet
8 feet

4.questionText: A fiberglass ladder should be used instead of a metal ladder when working near energized electrical equipment or wiring.

options.text: True
False

5.questionText: A stepladder's spreader will not lock. The task is short. What is the correct action?

options.text: Proceed carefully on the lower rungs only
Have a coworker hold the legs together during the task
Tag and remove the ladder from service, then obtain a properly functioning ladder
Brace the ladder against a wall to compensate for the unlocked spreader

6.questionText: What does maintaining three points of contact on a ladder mean?

options.text: Keeping three tools within reach at all times
Having two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, on the ladder at all times
Ensuring three rungs are within reach before moving
Touching the ladder with both feet and your chest for stability

7.questionText: Standing on the top cap or top step of a fully opened stepladder is permitted if no other option is available.

options.text: True
False

8.questionText: A worker on a ladder cannot reach the work area without leaning outside the side rails. What is the correct response?

options.text: Lean out while keeping one foot firmly on a rung
Move up one more rung to reduce the distance needed to reach
Hold a rail with one hand and extend the other arm as far as possible
Descend and reposition the ladder to allow safe access to the work area

9.questionText: A ladder is set up near a door that could swing open and hit it. What control is required before climbing?

options.text: Post a verbal warning to others in the area
Position the ladder so the door would only hit its side, not the front
Lock, block, or guard the door to prevent it from opening into the ladder
Assign a second worker to watch the door during the climb

10.questionText: A coworker has fallen from a ladder and may have injured their spine. The first action should be to move them to a more comfortable position.

options.text: True
False

11.questionText: Which combination of conditions would all justify stopping ladder use until the situation is corrected?

options.text: Clear skies, dry rungs, and a well-rested worker
Slight wind, wooden rungs, and a worker wearing gloves
Greasy rungs, a dizzy worker, and high winds
A new ladder, a level surface, and a short task

12.questionText: During a task, a ladder base shifts slightly on the ground but no one falls. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Finish the task since the ladder restabilized on its own
Watch the base more carefully for the rest of the task
Report it as a near miss and address the hazard before the ladder is used again
Include it in the end-of-week safety summary

13.questionText: At what minimum climb height does OSHA require fall protection on fixed ladders in construction?

options.text: 10 feet
16 feet
20 feet
24 feet

14.questionText: When carrying or moving a ladder through a construction site, workers must be especially alert for:

options.text: Floor marking tape that could snag the ladder feet
Overhead power lines, workers, vehicles, and building materials
Wet concrete that could damage the ladder feet
Other workers who might want to borrow the ladder

15.questionText: What does the 'belt buckle rule' tell a worker about body position while on a ladder?

options.text: A tool belt must be worn and buckled before climbing
The fall arrest anchor should be positioned at belt buckle height
The worker's belt buckle should remain between the ladder side rails
The belt buckle should face away from the ladder when stepping off at the top
